title: Network analysis of physical exercise, sleep quality, and psychological distress among Chinese university students
content:
by Jingbo Wang, Yuanyuan Ma, Tong Han, Juan Wang

Objective

Physical exercise, sleep quality, and psychological distress may be interconnected among university students, but their dimension-specific associations remain unclear. This study examined their network structure and compared male and female networks.

Methods

A convenience sample of 1,600 university students from two higher-education institutions in central China was surveyed from 16 March to 29 May 2026. Physical exercise, sleep quality, and psychological distress were assessed using the Physical Activity Rating Scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and 21-item Depression Anxiety Stress Scales. A 12-node regularized partial correlation network was estimated. Expected influence, bridge expected influence, bootstrap procedures, and network comparison tests were used.

Results

The network retained 27 non-zero edges, with stronger connections mainly within domains. Daytime dysfunction–stress had the largest positive cross-domain edge-weight point estimate, whereas exercise frequency–stress and exercise duration–subjective sleep quality were prominent negative connections. Stress showed relatively high expected influence and positive bridge expected influence point estimates, although bootstrap difference tests did not clearly distinguish these estimates from those of several other nodes. No gender-related differences were detected in global strength, network structure, or individual edges after multiple-comparison correction, while supplementary analyses indicated limited detection capability.

Conclusions

Cross-domain associations among physical exercise, sleep quality, and psychological distress were concentrated in a limited number of dimensions, particularly stress, daytime dysfunction, exercise frequency, and exercise duration. Stress and daytime dysfunction showed relatively prominent sleep–psychological distress associations, whereas higher exercise frequency and longer exercise duration were associated with lower stress and fewer subjective sleep problems, respectively. No gender-related network differences were detected, but this does not establish network equivalence. These cross-sectional findings identify dimension-specific associations but cannot establish causal relationships or intervention targets.
